title: Each transport demo is checked against a closed form or a balance: a Gaussian pulse for dispersion, an energy balance for heat transfer, and the Boltzmann law for ions near a charged wall
summary: Three single-physics demonstrations in micro-scale geometry: a solute pulse carried and spread along a channel, temperature in a heated channel wall and fluid, and the electric potential and ion concentrations next to a charged surface. Read each for the law it must obey, the numbers it prints, and whether the printed numbers are consistent with each other.

media.alt: Line plot of concentration against position from 0 to 2 millimetres. A single smooth bell-shaped pulse peaks at about 0.39 near x = 1.29 millimetres, with a width of about 0.3 millimetres at half height, and is zero outside 0.75 to 1.8 millimetres. The title gives mean speed 0.001 metres per second, effective diffusivity 2.9e-9 square metres per second and a Taylor-Aris coefficient of 1.9e-9.

source.note: The page teaches how to read a one-dimensional transport profile, a temperature field with an interface and an equilibrium double-layer profile using standard theory (Taylor-Aris dispersion, conjugate heat transfer, Poisson-Boltzmann). Numbers quoted are printed on the figures or computed in the Apply script, with assumptions named there.

read_the_figure.question: Does the computed pulse, temperature field or ion profile follow what the corresponding closed-form law or conservation statement says, and are the numbers in the title consistent with one another?
read_the_figure.axes: Dispersion: x is position along a channel in millimetres, y is a nondimensional concentration. Heat transfer: x is the streamwise coordinate from 0 to 200 micrometres, y the transverse coordinate from 0 to 25 micrometres; colour is temperature from about 300 to 400 K; a dashed cyan line at y = 20 micrometres marks the fluid/solid interface. Ion profile: x is distance from the charged wall in nanometres from 0 to 50; top y is potential in millivolts, bottom y is concentration divided by the bulk value for the positive and negative ion, with a dotted line at 1.
look_at: Dispersion: the pulse is symmetric and bell-shaped; its centre is displaced from the origin by about the mean speed times time, 1 mm.
Dispersion: the title's effective diffusivity exceeds the Taylor-Aris coefficient by 1.0e-9 m^2/s, which is a molecular diffusivity.
Heat transfer: cold fluid enters on the left at 300 K and warms towards the wall temperature of 400 K within about 100 micrometres; the interface line is at y = 20.
Heat transfer: the title gives a wall heat flow of 2171 W/m and an enthalpy rise of 83.63 W/m together with a balance residual of 5.33e-10.

Ion profile: the potential falls from -25 mV at the wall to zero over about 40 nm; the two potential curves lie on each other; the positive-ion curve rises to about 2.65 at the wall and the negative to about 0.375.
read_the_figure.proves: The dispersion figure shows a single smooth pulse of the expected shape in the right place. The heat-transfer figure shows the expected thermal entrance behaviour, but the two energy numbers in its title are not equal, so the balance claim is not shown by the title alone. The ion figure shows that the coupled-equation solution coincides with the equilibrium Boltzmann solution to 2.8 microvolts and gives wall concentrations that satisfy the Boltzmann factor.
if_wrong: A pulse displaced by far more or less than the mean speed times time: wrong velocity or an inlet condition error.
A pulse with a skewed or flat-topped shape at long time: numerical diffusion or dispersion from the transport scheme.
A temperature field with a kink at the interface: a conjugate coupling error; a heat balance that fails by a large factor: a wrong flux integral or boundary.
Potential curves that differ at the wall: a boundary condition error in one formulation; concentration ratios whose product is not 1 at equilibrium: charge or reference error.
must_check: The shape of the pulse is compared with the Gaussian it should be, not just inspected.
The time and distance scales are checked against h^2/D (Taylor regime) and U t (displacement).
Two energy quantities that are said to balance have the same boundary, units and sign.
The colour scale for a temperature field is bounded by the boundary temperatures and does not saturate across most of the domain.
For ion profiles, the Boltzmann factor is checked at the wall and the product of concentrations at equilibrium.
as_drawn: Dispersion: peak about 0.39 at x of about 1.29 mm; width at half height about 0.3 mm; title gives mean speed 0.001 m/s, effective diffusivity 2.9e-9 m^2/s, Taylor-Aris coefficient 1.9e-9 m^2/s, t = 1 s.

Heat transfer: colour range about 300 to 400 K; interface at y = 20 micrometres; cold column at the inlet over the whole height up to the interface; solid above the interface is already near 400 K away from the inlet. Title: wall heat 2171 W/m, enthalpy rise 83.63 W/m, balance residual 5.33e-10.

Ion profile: potential -25 mV at x = 0, about -9 mV at 10 nm, about -3 mV at 20 nm; maximum difference between the two formulations printed as 2.77e-06 V; concentrations 2.65 and about 0.375 at the wall, both returning to 1 beyond about 40 nm.

terms.meaning: The enhanced spreading of a solute along a channel because the parabolic velocity profile stretches it while cross-channel diffusion brings it back; for a long time the pulse spreads as if with a larger effective diffusivity.
The diffusion coefficient in the cross-section-averaged equation that reproduces the spread of the solute along the channel.
Heat transfer in which the temperature in the fluid and in the solid wall are solved together, with continuity of temperature and heat flux at the interface.
The length over which the temperature profile of a fluid entering a heated channel develops from uniform to its fully developed form.
The equilibrium model of the electric potential near a charged surface when ion concentrations follow the Boltzmann factor.
The transport model for ions: Nernst-Planck fluxes for each species coupled to the Poisson equation for the potential; at zero current it reduces to Poisson-Boltzmann.
The distance over which a charged surface is screened by the ions in a solution.

remember: A pulse that is only advected and diffused has a Gaussian shape; its centre moves at the mean speed and its variance grows as 2 D t.
The Taylor regime needs times longer than the cross-channel diffusion time h^2/D.
An energy balance compares like with like: same boundary, same units.
At equilibrium a full transport model collapses to a simpler one, so agreement tests the code, not the physics.
Concentrations at a charged wall follow exp of minus charge times potential over thermal energy.

understand.title: A pulse that translates and spreads
understand.text: The cross-section-averaged concentration obeys a one-dimensional advection-diffusion equation with the effective diffusivity. A Gaussian initial pulse stays Gaussian: its centre moves by the mean speed times time and its variance grows by two times the diffusivity times time. The figure shows a displacement of about one millimetre, equal to 0.001 m/s times 1 s.

understand.title: Taylor-Aris and the title's numbers
understand.text: The effective diffusivity is the molecular value plus the Taylor-Aris term. The title's 2.9e-9 and 1.9e-9 differ by 1.0e-9, a typical small-molecule value. For a plane channel the Taylor-Aris term is two one-hundred-and-fifth of the square of the product of mean speed and half-width, divided by the molecular diffusivity; with 1e-9 for the molecular value it gives a half-width of 10 micrometres, the size of the gaps in other microfluidics figures. The inference uses an assumed molecular diffusivity.

understand.title: What the temperature field shows
understand.text: Fluid enters cold, the heated solid warms it from the wall inward and the temperature approaches the wall value within about 100 micrometres: the thermal entrance region. The flux through the wall is large near the inlet and decays downstream. The colour scale tops out at the wall temperature, so almost the whole domain downstream is a single yellow.

understand.title: Why the energy numbers need a check
understand.text: In steady state with insulated outer faces the heat entering the fluid through the interface equals the enthalpy carried out by the fluid. The title gives 2171 W/m for the wall heat and 83.63 W/m for the enthalpy rise, a ratio of 26. Either they refer to different surfaces or the balance residual refers to something else; the title does not say.

understand.title: Why PNP and PB agree
understand.text: With no current and no applied field the ions are in equilibrium and their fluxes vanish, so the Nernst-Planck equations give the Boltzmann distribution and the system becomes the Poisson-Boltzmann equation. Matching it tests that the coupled discretisation reproduces its own limit. It does not test the transport physics away from equilibrium.

steps.title: Advection-diffusion of the average
steps.tex: \frac{\partial\bar C}{\partial t}+\bar U\frac{\partial\bar C}{\partial x}=D_\mathrm{eff}\frac{\partial^{2}\bar C}{\partial x^{2}}
steps.note: The cross-section average of the concentration, with the mean speed and the effective diffusivity.

steps.title: Gaussian pulse
steps.note: Centre displaced by the mean speed times time; variance grows by 2 D t.

steps.title: Taylor-Aris coefficient, plane channel
steps.note: h is the channel half-width. The Taylor regime needs t much larger than h^2/D_m.

steps.title: Steady energy balance
steps.note: Heat entering the fluid across the interface per unit depth equals the enthalpy flow out minus in, if all other faces are adiabatic.

steps.title: Boltzmann ion concentrations
steps.note: For monovalent ions. At the wall psi is -25 mV, thermal voltage about 25.7 mV, so c_+ is about 2.65 c_0 and c_- about 0.378 c_0.

steps.title: Gouy-Chapman potential
steps.note: The exact solution of Poisson-Boltzmann next to a flat wall in a symmetric 1:1 electrolyte.

worked.title: Recover the channel size and the regime from the dispersion title
worked.problem: The title gives mean speed 0.001 m/s, D_eff = 2.9e-9 m^2/s, Taylor-Aris K = 1.9e-9 m^2/s and t = 1 s. Assume the plane-channel formula for K. What molecular diffusivity and half-width does that imply, and is t long enough for the Taylor regime?

solution.text: Cross-channel diffusion time against the elapsed time.

worked.answer: A molecular diffusivity of 1e-9 m^2/s and a half-width of 10 micrometres, a 20 micrometre gap; t is ten times the diffusion time, so the Taylor regime is reasonable but not deep. This reconstructs the numbers from round values, an inference rather than a printed fact.

analyze.q: The pulse's half-height width is about 0.3 mm, which gives a standard deviation of about 0.13 mm. With D_eff of 2.9e-9 and t of 1 s, how much of the variance comes from diffusion and how much from the initial pulse?
analyze.hint: 2 D t is 5.8e-9 m^2; the observed variance is about 1.6e-8 m^2.

analyze.q: In the heat-transfer figure the colour scale saturates at 400 K over most of the domain. What features of the field are hidden, and what plot would show them?
analyze.hint: Consider a log of the temperature deficit or profiles at selected x.

analyze.q: Both ion concentrations in the lower panel return to 1 within about 40 nm, while the potential curve has fallen to about 3 mV at 20 nm. What does the ratio of the two scales suggest about the nonlinearity of the profile?
analyze.hint: Compare e psi over kT with 1.

evaluate.q: The title of the heat-transfer figure quotes a balance residual of 5.33e-10 beside two energy numbers that differ by a factor of 26. What would you ask the author to add so the claim is checkable?
evaluate.hint: Which surfaces are integrated, and what is the residual relative to.

evaluate.q: The ion figure compares PNP with PB and reports 2.77 microvolts. Is that a test of the Poisson-Boltzmann physics, of the PNP discretisation, or of both?
evaluate.hint: The two models are equivalent at equilibrium.

create: Design a one-panel plot that shows the dispersion pulse together with its Gaussian prediction and the residual between them, with a second curve for pure diffusion (without the Taylor term) so the effect of the term is visible.

Specify the check you would add to the heat-transfer demo: a quantity integrated on a stated boundary, its analytic expectation for a simple limiting case (for example, uniform wall temperature and slug flow) and the plot that shows the error.

checks.q: Why is the effective diffusivity larger than the molecular one in a pressure-driven channel?
checks.hint: What does the parabolic profile do to a solute plug?
checks.answer: The velocity differences stretch the plug along the channel while cross-channel diffusion samples different velocities, adding a term that grows with the square of the speed and the channel width.

checks.q: What is the Taylor-Aris coefficient for U = 1e-3 m/s, h = 10 micrometres and D_m = 1e-9 m^2/s?
The Boltzmann factors at the wall are 2.65 and 0.378. What is their product, and why?
checks.answer: Their product is about 1.0, because exp(+x) times exp(-x) is 1 for equal and opposite valence.

checks.q: The heat-transfer title has numbers of 2171 and 83.63 W/m. Does the figure show a heat balance?
checks.answer: No; they differ by about 26 times, so either they refer to different surfaces or the balance is not satisfied; the title needs to state the integrated surfaces.

checks.q: How would you make the dispersion figure a test and not a picture?
checks.answer: Overlay the analytic Gaussian with the same displacement and variance, plot the residual, and repeat at several times to show the variance growing as 2 D t.

The page does not repeat the solver name. No PLACEHOLDER footer or thesis remark seen in these three. Owner review: (1) the CHT title gives q_wall = 2171 W/m and enthalpy_rise = 83.63 W/m, which differ by a factor of about 26 although they sit beside a 'balance residual' of 5.33e-10; the figure does not say what is integrated. (2) The CHT colour scale saturates at 400 K across most of the domain, hiding the downstream field. (3) The dispersion figure shows a single time; its D_eff = D_m + K decomposition is inferred here from the printed numbers (D_m = 1e-9 m^2/s and half-width 10 micrometres are not printed). (4) The pulse's initial width and start position are not stated. (5) The ion figure's concentration curves are not compared with an independent analytic curve; the PB comparison is for the potential only.
